meta.contactLevel: moderate (tackling, shoulder-to-shoulder, aerial contests; less than rugby)
meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 1 match/week typical; congested championship/league weeks up to 2
meta.notes: Amateur sport at all levels (no professional contracts) — players hold jobs/study, so total weekly load and recovery time are the binding constraints. Pitch is large (~140 x 85 m), larger than soccer, driving high total running volume.

maxStrength.why: Underpins power, contact tolerance and robustness, but football is not strength-limited — strength serves speed/power and injury resistance, not an end in itself.
maxStrength.source: Suchomel 2016 (strength as a foundation for athletic performance)

relativeStrength.why: Strength-to-bodyweight drives acceleration, jumping and tackling without adding mass that slows repeated running.

explosivePower.why: Kicking distance/accuracy, breaking from a standstill, and aerial fielding all depend on lower-body power output.
explosivePower.source: Reilly & Collins 2008 (Science and the Gaelic sports); expert consensus

reactiveStrength.why: Repeated jump-land in aerial contests and fast COD rely on the stretch-shortening cycle; also a marker of tendon stiffness/efficiency.

sprintSpeed.why: Top speed separates attackers/defenders in open pitch and on breaks; high-speed running exposure is also where most hamstrings tear.
sprintSpeed.source: Malone et al. 2017 (high-speed running & injury, Gaelic football)

acceleration.why: Most efforts are short bursts to lose/track a marker, win a breaking ball, or attack a gap — 0-10 m acceleration is used constantly.
acceleration.source: Malone et al. 2016/2017 (GPS demands of elite Gaelic football)

deceleration.why: Tackling, turning and stopping under control; poor eccentric braking is a knee/hamstring/ankle injury driver.

changeOfDirection.why: Solo running, sidestepping a tackle and tracking attackers demand rapid multidirectional COD.

aerobicEndurance.why: 70+ min on a large pitch with ~8-9 km covered per game; aerobic fitness also protects against ACWR spikes.
aerobicEndurance.source: Malone et al. 2017 (aerobic fitness moderates injury risk in Gaelic football)

anaerobicEndurance.why: Repeated high-intensity efforts with incomplete recovery tax the glycolytic system, especially late in halves.
anaerobicEndurance.source: Cullen et al. (physiological demands of Gaelic football)

repeatSprintAbility.why: The defining fitness quality: many maximal/near-maximal sprints with short recovery across the game.
repeatSprintAbility.source: Malone et al. 2016 (running demands); expert consensus

mobility.why: Hip and ankle range support kicking mechanics and safe deceleration; a means to robustness, not a performance end.

stability.why: Single-leg control for kicking, landing and contact; lumbopelvic control underpins force transfer and back/groin health.

rotationalPower.why: Kicking and hand-passing transfer force through a rotating trunk; secondary to linear power in football (primary in hurling).

gripStrength.why: High-catch fielding and possession in the tackle, but lower demand than stick sports.

neckStrength.why: Aerial collisions and tackles carry some head-contact exposure; lower priority than collision codes but relevant for concussion mitigation.
neckStrength.source: expert consensus (cf. World Rugby neck guidance)

balance.why: Landing from contested catches, one-leg kicking and contact all demand dynamic balance.

coordination.why: Catching, kicking off both feet, soloing and hand-passing under pressure are high skill-coordination demands.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: ~1:4 to 1:6 (intermittent; brief high-intensity efforts with active recovery)
energySystems.matchDemands: ~8-9 km total distance; high-speed running ~600-1000 m; repeated accelerations/decelerations; aerial contests; intermittent profile across 2 x 35 min.
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Mean ~85% HRmax; sustained periods >90% HRmax during intense phases.
energySystems.fatigueProfile: High-speed running and acceleration counts decline in the final quarter; late-game fatigue raises injury risk — a key reason for conditioning + load management.
energySystems.source: Reilly & Collins 2008; Malone et al. 2016 (GPS demands); Cullen et al. — estimates, vary by level/position
energySystems.notes: Estimates synthesised from inter-county GPS/HR studies; club-level demands are lower. Treat percentages as indicative, not exact.

movementProfile.jointLoading: High eccentric load at knee/hip in deceleration and landing; hamstrings loaded at end-range during sprinting and kicking; ankle dorsiflexion/inversion stress on cuts.
movementProfile.groundContacts: Many high-velocity ground contacts (sprinting + landings); studded boots on grass.
movementProfile.landingDemands: Repeated single- and double-leg landings from contested high catches — a key ACL/ankle exposure.
movementProfile.throwing: None (hand-pass is a striking action, not an overhead throw).
movementProfile.jumping: Frequent maximal vertical/contested jumps for high ball.
movementProfile.cutting: Frequent sharp cuts and sidesteps (solo running, evading tackles).
movementProfile.rotating: Moderate (kicking, hand-passing, turning to track runners).
movementProfile.overheadActions: High catching with arms overhead under contact.
movementProfile.collisions: Shoulder-to-shoulder challenges, blocks and tackles — moderate collision load.
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: Repetitive footstrike + landings; cumulative lower-limb tendon/bone load.
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Kicking-leg dominance and turning-side preference create left-right asymmetries to monitor.
commonDeficiencies: posterior-chain strength relative to running volume

common.name: Hamstring strain
common.rtpConsiderations: Progressive sprint reloading + eccentric strength restoration; objective high-speed-running tolerance before full return.
common.source: GAA injury surveillance (Roe/Murphy/Blake); Malone et al. 2017; van Dyk 2019 (eccentric strength & hamstring injury)

common.name: Ankle sprain (lateral)
common.mechanism: landing on another foot / cutting with inversion
common.rtpConsiderations: Balance/proprioception + return-to-run/cut progression; consider bracing/taping early.
common.source: GAA injury surveillance; IOC ankle-sprain consensus

common.name: Knee — ACL rupture
common.rtpConsiderations: 9-12 month criteria-based RTP; LSI >90% strength + hop battery + psychological readiness.
common.source: FIFA 11+ / neuromuscular-training ACL-prevention literature; Arundale RTP consensus

common.name: Concussion
common.mechanism: head contact in aerial challenges, tackles, collisions
common.rtpConsiderations: Graduated return-to-sport per concussion consensus (Amsterdam/CISG); medical clearance mandatory.

injuryProfile.summary: Hamstring is the headline modifiable target; ACL is the headline severity target. Most are lower-limb, fatigue- and load-sensitive — the core argument for the load-management + prevention sections.

positions.name: Goalkeeper
positions.role: Shot-stopping, kick-outs (restart strategy), sweeping behind defence.
positions.movementDemands: Low total distance; explosive dives, short reactions; long kick-out striking.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Lowest running load — can tolerate more gym emphasis.

positions.name: Full-back line (corner-back / full-back)
positions.role: Man-marking, defending the inside line, contesting high ball.
positions.movementDemands: Reactive man-marking; repeated short sprints + aerial contests.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: High accel/decel load — manage eccentric soreness.

positions.name: Half-back line
positions.role: Defend then drive forward as a primary attacking outlet; high two-way running.
positions.movementDemands: Box-to-box; among the highest distances and high-speed running.
gymPriorities: max strength maintained at low volume in-season
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest running load with midfield — protect from HSR spikes.

positions.name: Midfield
positions.role: Win kick-outs (aerial), link defence and attack, cover the most ground.
positions.movementDemands: Highest total distance + frequent maximal jumps for kick-outs.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest combined running + jump-land load — the most load-sensitive group.

positions.name: Half-forward line
positions.role: Two-way running forwards: score, create, and track back to defend.
positions.movementDemands: High two-way running with repeated sprints into space.

positions.name: Full-forward line (corner-forward / full-forward)
positions.role: Inside scorers: lose markers over short distances, finish chances.
positions.movementDemands: Short explosive movements, sidesteps, contested catches.
positions.runningDemands: Moderate (lowest of outfield); high acceleration density.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Lower running load than half-lines — tolerates more power/strength emphasis.

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ)
assessments.purpose: Lower-body power + neuromuscular fatigue monitoring (drop in jump height/flight-time vs baseline flags fatigue).
equipment: jump mat or force plate / Nordbord-style

assessments.name: 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test (30-15 IFT)
assessments.purpose: Intermittent aerobic capacity + sets individualised conditioning velocities (VIFT).

assessments.name: Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test (Level 1)
assessments.purpose: Intermittent endurance with recovery — common GAA field test.

assessments.name: 10 m / 20 m / 40 m sprint (timing gates)
assessments.purpose: Acceleration (10 m) and max-velocity (40 m) qualities; flying-10 for top speed.

assessments.name: Nordic hamstring eccentric strength (Nordbord)
assessments.purpose: Eccentric hamstring strength + left-right asymmetry — a modifiable hamstring-injury risk factor.

assessments.name: Isometric adductor / groin squeeze
assessments.purpose: Adductor strength + monitoring (drop flags groin-injury risk).

targets.elite: track vs individual baseline (>10% drop = caution)

assessments.name: Isometric mid-thigh pull (IMTP)
assessments.purpose: Maximal force / RFD with minimal fatigue cost.

assessments.name: Return-to-play hop battery + strength LSI
assessments.purpose: Criteria-based clearance after lower-limb injury (esp. ACL/hamstring).

targets.elite: LSI >90% strength + hop symmetry; sport-specific running tolerance

assessments.source: Arundale 2018 RTP consensus; van Dyk RTP

youth.trainingEmphasis: Athletic literacy, bodyweight strength, sprint mechanics, multi-sport exposure; bone/tissue development.

development.trainingEmphasis: Build a strength + tissue-capacity base; introduce structured load monitoring; running mechanics.
commonMistakes: chasing match performance over building capacity

senior.trainingEmphasis: Maintain physical qualities at minimal effective volume while peaking for matches; protect availability.

elite.trainingEmphasis: Individualised, data-led maintenance + targeted development of each player's limiter; squad fixture-driven periodisation.

masters.trainingEmphasis: Retain strength/power (use it or lose it), manage recovery and connective-tissue load, longer recovery windows.

offSeason.primaryObjective: Build max strength + physical-quality base; address individual limiters and prior injuries.
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Max strength, hypertrophy where needed, aerobic base, eccentric/robustness work.

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert strength to power/speed; build match conditioning + RSA; taper into competition.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: Power, speed, RSA, sport-specific conditioning; reduce gym volume as pitch load rises.

competition.primaryObjective: Maintain physical qualities at minimal effective volume; maximise match availability/freshness.
competition.trainingEmphasis: Heavy-but-low-volume strength maintenance, short power/speed exposures, prevention work; conditioning topped up by matches/pitch.
competition.intensity: high (low volume preserves quality without fatigue)

playoffs.primaryObjective: Peak freshness + availability for knockout matches.
playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Minimal-volume high-intensity maintenance; sharpening; heavy prioritisation of recovery.
testingRecommendations: readiness monitoring only — no fatiguing tests

recovery.primaryObjective: Physical and mental recovery; restore tissue; address niggles.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: Unstructured activity, mobility, light cross-training; rehab of carried injuries.
testingRecommendations: none (rest); medical review of carried injuries

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: MD (match day) anchored; gym placed early in the week, recovery late.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: MD-4 or MD-3 (lower-body strength, far from match)
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: embedded in warm-ups daily; primary dose MD-4/MD-3
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: MD+1 recovery → MD-4 high → MD-3 moderate/power → MD-2 sharpen → MD-1 activation → MD.

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: Recovery-first: no separate heavy gym day; maintenance only between matches.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: optional micro-dose between matches if >72 h gap
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Match → recovery → light activation → Match → recovery. Cut gym volume ~40-50%.
avoidHeavyLiftingDays: all days between two matches in the same week
preferExplosiveWorkDays: only a brief priming dose pre-match if used

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: Pure availability management; minimise all non-essential load.
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect recovery between fixtures; gym is maintenance/priming, never development.

transfersWell: sprint training (as the primary speed tool)
limitedValue: bodybuilding isolation for its own sake
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: High — football is played on one leg (running, kicking, landing); single-leg strength + control is a priority for performance and knee/hamstring health.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: Optional/advanced — useful for RFD if technically competent, but loaded/trap-bar jumps and sprinting give much of the benefit at lower technical/fatigue cost. Not essential for most players.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: Moderate-high but dosed — landing mechanics, bilateral then unilateral, progressed off a strength base; manage volume given high running impact load.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: Train the trunk to resist (anti-rotation, anti-extension, anti-lateral-flexion) for force transfer in kicking/contact; minimal high-volume flexion crunching.
gymPhilosophy.neckTraining: Low-dose isometric neck work as concussion-mitigation insurance; lower priority than collision codes.
gymPhilosophy.gripTraining: Low priority (some fielding benefit); not a limiter in football.
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: Moderate — med-ball rotational throws support kicking/hand-pass power and trunk force transfer.
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Useful in-season + rehab: low-fatigue strength maintenance (e.g. iso split squats, adductor/hamstring isos) and tendon load management.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Controlled eccentrics for hypertrophy/robustness phases; explosive concentric intent for power phases; avoid grinding near matches.
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Use bar-velocity / intent cues: heavy-fast for strength-speed, lighter-faster for speed-strength; consider VBT autoregulation in-season to cap fatigue.

exercisesToAvoid: max-effort sprinting when fatigued or under-prepared
introducing long-lever Copenhagen at high volume too quickly
return to cutting before balance restored
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: IOC ankle-sprain prevention literature; balance-training meta-analyses

decisionRules.then: remove high-soreness exercises (Nordic, heavy eccentric, novel plyometrics); allow only low-fatigue priming
gym is priming only (low-volume CNS power, e.g. a few jumps/throws) or rest; no strength development

decisionRules.if: athlete reports high hamstring soreness OR Nordbord force drop >15% vs baseline
decisionRules.then: reduce/skip eccentric hamstring loading and high-speed running; substitute isometric/low-load hamstring work; flag for review
reduce change-of-direction + kicking volume and progress adductor load conservatively; monitor daily

decisionRules.if: two matches occur in the same week
decisionRules.then: reduce gym volume by ~40-50% and remove the heavy day; keep only maintenance + prevention
cap or reduce high-speed-running and total load this week; avoid adding gym conditioning volume
rebuild load gradually (do not spike); reintroduce high-speed running progressively

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + high soreness + low subjective wellness)
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down: reduce intensity/volume one step, prioritise technique + recovery; do not test
treat as neuromuscular fatigue: reduce high-CNS/plyometric load, emphasise recovery, recheck next session

decisionRules.if: athlete reports systemic illness (fever / below-neck symptoms)
decisionRules.then: withhold training until symptom-free; resume gradually

decisionRules.if: long-haul travel / significant time-zone shift in last 24-48 h
decisionRules.then: reduce session intensity and prioritise sleep/hydration; defer testing
hold strength at minimal effective volume (heavy, low sets, far from match day); do not chase PRs

acwr.model: acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) workload ratio; rolling/EWMA preferred
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016; Malone 2017 (Gaelic football) — methodology contested (Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019), treat as a soft monitoring input not a hard rule

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10-15% week-to-week spikes in total/high-speed running load; aerobic fitness moderates spike risk (build the base).

gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low maintenance (1-2 sessions; ~6-10 hard sets/wk per region)

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~1 heavy session/week sustains lower-body strength in-season (low volume, high intensity preserves the quality with minimal fatigue).
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season development window — push volume here, not in-season.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by amateur lifestyle + pitch load; gym must never compromise pitch performance — the binding ceiling is total athlete load, not gym MRV alone.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload roughly every 3-5 weeks in development phases; auto-deload when fatigue markers (CMJ drop, high soreness, ACWR >1.5) accumulate.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress load when reps/quality met at target RPE and readiness is green; prefer adding intensity over volume in-season.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On red readiness or fixture congestion, drop one step (volume first, then intensity); never both heavy gym + heavy pitch on the same day.
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Do not 'make up' missed sessions by stacking load; resume at planned level. After ≥2 weeks off, rebuild gradually (re-enter at reduced load).
loadManagement.source: Gabbett 2016; Malone 2017; Rønnestad in-season strength; expert consensus

factors.name: Subjective wellness (soreness/energy/mood)
factors.source: Saw 2016 (subjective measures often more sensitive than objective)

thresholds.modifier: cut eccentric/HSR or COD load for that tissue
treat as accumulating fatigue; ease load
reduce load; amateur athletes carry job/study load

readinessModel.notes: Subjective wellness + sleep + prior load carry the most weight; objective vitals (HRV/RHR) are trend signals, not single-day triggers. The readiness score rolls these into one number — and CRUCIALLY, the raw vitals stay private to the athlete; a coach sees only the derived readiness score (see TEAM-ARCHITECTURE.md).

coachDashboard.principle: Coach sees DERIVED and availability signals only — never an individual's raw HRV/sleep/resting-HR. Aggregated, plain-English, action-oriented.
coachDashboard.trafficLightIndicators: Per-player green/amber/red from the derived readiness + load state (no underlying numbers shown).
coachDashboard.privacyNote: All per-athlete entries here are DERIVED (readiness score, load_state, ACWR, adherence %, injury availability). Raw vitals are excluded by design and enforced by the schema validator.

educationTips: why eccentric hamstring work matters for sprinting
why in-season strength is low-volume not zero
what your readiness colour means today

strongEvidence: eccentric hamstring training reduces hamstring injury (van Dyk 2019; Petersen 2011)
neuromuscular warm-ups reduce ACL/lower-limb injury (FIFA 11+ meta-analyses)
Copenhagen adductor work reduces groin injury (Harøy 2019)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness measure (Saw 2016)
strength can be maintained in-season at low volume (Rønnestad)
weakEvidence: exact ACWR thresholds (0.8/1.3/1.5) — contested methodology (Impellizzeri 2020, Lolli 2019)
single-day HRV/RHR as a training trigger
areasRequiringExpertJudgement: individual MRV / total-load ceiling for amateur athletes with jobs
when to override the model for a key player
areasRequiringFutureResearch: long-term effects of amateur dual-load (job + sport)
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: treating ACWR as a hard rule could under- or over-train players
removing all in-season strength (qualities decay, injury risk rises)
exposing raw vitals to coaches (privacy + trust breach)
prescribing high-soreness work too close to matches

kpis.name: Readiness
kpis.measurementMethod: Composite of subjective wellness + sleep + prior load (+ optional HRV trend), normalised to individual baseline
kpis.source: Saw 2016; derived score (raw vitals stay private)

kpis.name: Lower-body power (CMJ)
kpis.targetRange: ≥40 cm (elite male); within 10% of baseline for fatigue

kpis.name: Resting HR
kpis.measurementMethod: Morning resting heart rate vs baseline
kpis.source: expert consensus (PRIVATE — athlete-only; rolls into readiness)

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Readiness
athleteDashboardKpis.why: One daily number that tells the player whether to push or back off — actionable and motivating.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Weekly consistency
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Rewards showing up; consistency beats occasional perfect weeks for long-term development.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Strength progression
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Visible proof the gym work is paying off — the clearest motivator for adherence.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Speed/power score
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Directly tied to on-pitch performance the player cares about.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Recovery score
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Teaches the player that recovery is training; nudges sleep/soreness habits.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Hamstring/groin resilience
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Turns invisible prevention work into a tracked, improving score — the injuries that cost them most.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Conditioning (RSA) score
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Game-fitness trend the player feels every match; ties testing to match performance.

athleteDashboardKpis.name: Availability streak
athleteDashboardKpis.why: Celebrates injury-free time on the pitch — the ultimate goal, framed positively.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Team readiness
coachDashboardKpis.why: At-a-glance squad freshness (traffic-light, derived) to shape the session before it starts.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Training availability
coachDashboardKpis.why: Who is fit / modified / out — the single most important planning input.

coachDashboardKpis.name: High-risk athlete flags
coachDashboardKpis.why: Surfaces the few players needing attention (ACWR spike, red readiness, monitoring drop).

coachDashboardKpis.name: Weekly workload distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Shows who is over/under-loaded across the squad to balance the week.

coachDashboardKpis.name: ACWR distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Flags spike-risk players (soft input) so load can be adjusted proactively.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Position-group load comparison
coachDashboardKpis.why: Midfield/half-lines carry more — lets the coach load groups appropriately.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Training completion / compliance
coachDashboardKpis.why: Shows whether prescribed gym + prevention is actually being done.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Match readiness
coachDashboardKpis.why: Squad freshness/availability heading into the match — selection + taper decisions.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Recovery trend (team)
coachDashboardKpis.why: Derived readiness trend warns of accumulating fatigue across a block.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Injury/illness status summary
coachDashboardKpis.why: Availability picture (status only, no private detail) for planning + medical liaison.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Prevention-work compliance
coachDashboardKpis.why: Whether the hamstring/groin/ACL programmes are being done — the controllable injury lever.

coachDashboardKpis.name: Fatigue distribution
coachDashboardKpis.why: Spread of green/amber/red shows if the whole squad or just individuals are cooked.

performanceScore.philosophy: Reflects progress toward the demands of Gaelic football, weighted to the qualities that matter most, rewarding consistency and availability and penalising excessive fatigue/poor recovery — never rewarding unsafe training.

components.rationale: Consistency drives long-term development; rewarded over occasional perfect weeks.
Being fit to play is the point; availability is the strongest performance lever.
Aerobic/RSA is the defining match-fitness quality.
Speed/power separate players in open play.
Eccentric hamstring/adductor capacity — protective and trainable.
Penalises chronic fatigue/poor recovery; keeps the score honest about sustainability.

guardrails: never increases for training through red readiness or injury
consistency + availability dominate so the score can't be gamed by occasional max efforts
fatigue/recovery acts as a multiplier that caps the score when recovery is poor
performanceScore.explainability: Each component is shown with its contribution so the athlete sees exactly why the score moved and what to work on next.

gamification.name: Injury-free weeks
gamification.rewards: Recognition for consecutive weeks available + completing prevention work — ties motivation to robustness, not just workouts.

gamification.name: Consistency streak
gamification.rewards: Unbroken weeks hitting prescribed sessions; rewards process over outcome.

gamification.name: Prevention badge
gamification.rewards: Completing the hamstring/groin/ACL programme each week — makes the unglamorous work visible.

gamification.name: Testing-battery completion
gamification.rewards: Completing each testing block (CMJ/sprint/30-15/Nordbord) — encourages objective tracking.

gamification.name: Personal-best milestones
gamification.rewards: Sprint/CMJ/strength PRs vs the player's own baseline — self-referenced, not leaderboard.

gamification.name: Sport-specific milestones
gamification.rewards: Reaching position-relevant benchmarks (e.g. midfielder hits target VIFT) — rewards becoming more capable in the sport.

gamification.name: Long-term development arc
gamification.rewards: Season-over-season capability growth chart — frames the long game over short-term grinding.
